grammarPoints.title: Verb classes and polite conjugation
grammarPoints.meaning: Japanese verbs fall into three classes, and class determines how the polite stem is formed. The polite forms let a speaker choose an appropriate level of formality.
grammarPoints.formation: Ru-verbs drop final る and add ます／ません. U-verbs change the final u-row sound to the matching i-row sound before ます／ません. Irregular する becomes します／しません, and 来る becomes 来ます／来ません (きます／きません).
notes: The dictionary form identifies a verb but is not the polite sentence ending used in these exercises.
Learn a verb’s class with the verb; some verbs ending in る are class 1.
This point focuses on how the form is made. The common meanings of polite nonpast are the next point.
The polite stem is the part before ます: 読み, 食べ, し, and き. Do not classify every verb ending in る as a ru-verb.

schemas.context: A teacher asks what each participant does during a free activity period. State the activity.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: These activities can naturally appear without an explicit object. Use a polite verb, not verb + です.

schemas.context: Explain what a participant does not do during the free activity period.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: The negative polite verb ends in ません.

schemas.context: Practise the u-verb, ru-verb and irregular classes.
schemas.english: Give the polite affirmative and polite negative forms of the verb meaning “{verb}”.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: This supplementary drill isolates endings; the other exercises use full sentences.

grammarPoints.title: Present/nonpast meaning of verbs
grammarPoints.meaning: The polite nonpast covers repeated habits and actions expected or planned for the future. It does not normally mean that an action is happening right now.
grammarPoints.formation: Use a polite verb form for affirmative nonpast and the polite negative form for a negative nonpast sentence. Context and time words distinguish habit from future.
notes: Japanese verbs do not change for person or number.
A nonpast sentence can describe a routine or a future plan; use context to show which.
Do not use this form alone to say an action is in progress.

examples.japanese: ユイさんは勉強します。
examples.kana: ユイさんはべんきょうします。

schemas.context: Describe the participant’s usual activity during a free period.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: The context makes this a habit, not an action in progress.

schemas.context: Describe the participant’s plan for the next free period.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: The same Japanese nonpast form can describe a future plan.

schemas.context: Describe an activity someone does not do during free periods.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Negate the verb with ません.

schemas.context: Explain the participant’s plan for the next free period.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Context gives ません a future negative meaning.

grammarPoints.title: を, で, に, and へ with verbs
grammarPoints.meaning: を marks a direct object, で the place where an action happens, に a destination or arrival point, and へ the direction toward which someone goes.
grammarPoints.formation: Place the particle-marked phrase before the verb: [topic] は [time] [destination] に/へ [place] で [object] を verb. Use に or へ with movement verbs, and で with an action location.
notes: を is pronounced お.
へ is pronounced え when used as a particle.
The destination and action location have different roles; avoid marking the destination with で in a simple movement sentence.
Word order is flexible, but particles show the roles and the verb usually comes last.
来る describes movement toward the speaker’s location; 行く describes movement away. English “I’m coming to you” may therefore require 行きます.

examples.english: I study Japanese at the library.
examples.japanese: 私は図書館で日本語を勉強します。
examples.kana: わたしはとしょかんでにほんごをべんきょうします。

examples.japanese: ケンタさんは店に行きます。
examples.kana: ケンタさんはみせにいきます。

schemas.instruction: Write the sentence in Japanese, marking the action place and object.
schemas.context: Describe a polite study or reading activity.
schemas.omission: Topic and action place can be omitted if already established.
restrictions: Use で for the place where studying happens; use を for the subject studied.
This schema uses the lexical verb 勉強する in its polite form.

schemas.context: Describe a regular trip away from the speaker’s location.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: に and へ both mark this destination. Time に cannot be replaced by へ. Transportation で is not required here.

schemas.context: You are already at {destination}. Report another person’s plan to join you there.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Use 来る because movement is toward the speaker’s location.

schemas.context: Describe a return to a familiar base after an outing.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: 帰る means return to a base such as home or one’s school; do not use it for every destination.

grammarPoints.title: Time expressions with に
grammarPoints.meaning: に marks a specific time when an action occurs. Many relative or broad time expressions do not take に.
grammarPoints.formation: Specific clock times, days, and dates + に; expressions such as today, tomorrow, every day, and relative time periods normally appear without に.
notes: Use に with clock times and days of the week. Relative words such as 今日／明日, repeated intervals such as 毎日, and いつ do not take に.
Parts of the day and 週末 usually appear without に; に is possible with a different emphasis or style.
Use ごろ for an approximate clock time: time ごろ or time ごろに. It is different from duration ぐらい in Lesson 4.

examples.japanese: 私は七時に晩ご飯を食べます。
examples.kana: わたしはしちじにばんごはんをたべます。
わたしはまいにちべんきょうします。

schemas.context: State a regular schedule.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: The time lexeme contains no に; the schema adds it.

schemas.context: Describe someone’s routine.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Use these time expressions without に in this model.

schemas.context: Give an approximate schedule.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Use ごろ for clock time; ごろに is also possible.

schemas.context: Ask about a planned trip.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Do not put に after いつ. The に in this sentence marks the destination.

grammarPoints.title: Inviting with ませんか
grammarPoints.meaning: A polite negative question can gently invite the listener to do an activity together.
grammarPoints.formation: Verb polite-negative form + か. The invitation commonly includes the listener contextually, so a separate ‘you’ is unnecessary.
notes: This is an invitation, not simply a question asking whether the listener does not act.
Use an activity the speaker and listener can reasonably do together.
ちょっと… can gently decline an invitation by leaving the difficulty unstated; いいですね can accept enthusiastically.

examples.english: Won't you have lunch with me?
examples.japanese: 一緒に昼ご飯を食べませんか。
examples.kana: いっしょにひるごはんをたべませんか。

schemas.context: Invite a classmate to share an activity.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Use ませんか for an invitation; ますか simply asks about their plans. 一緒に is a fixed expression here.

schemas.context: Invite a friend on a trip away from your current location.
schemas.english: Would you like to go to {destination} together {time}?
schemas.kana: {time}いっしょに{destination}にいきませんか。
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: The subject is understood to include the speaker and listener.

schemas.context: Someone has invited you out on {day}. Decline gently using the customary unfinished response.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: ちょっと leaves the inconvenient reason unsaid; a blunt いいえ is usually avoided.

grammarPoints.title: Frequency adverbs
grammarPoints.meaning: Frequency words describe how often an action happens. Most occur before the verb; ぜんぜん and あまり normally accompany a negative predicate.
grammarPoints.formation: Topic + frequency adverb + (time/place/object phrases) + verb. Pair ぜんぜん／あまり with a negative verb.
notes: よく means often; ときどき means sometimes; あまり and ぜんぜん mean not very often / not at all when paired with a negative.
Do not use the marked negative adverbs with an affirmative verb in the beginner pattern.

examples.japanese: 私はよく映画を見ます。
examples.kana: わたしはよくえいがをみます。

examples.english: I do not drink tea very often.
examples.japanese: 私はあまりお茶を飲みません。
examples.kana: わたしはあまりおちゃをのみません。

schemas.context: Explain a reading or studying habit.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Use an affirmative frequency adverb with the affirmative verb.

schemas.context: Explain how infrequently someone reads or studies.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: あまり means not very often/much with the negative; ぜんぜん means not at all.

grammarPoints.title: Basic Japanese word order
grammarPoints.meaning: Japanese sentences normally put the verb at the end. Time, place, and object phrases usually come before it, while particles make their roles clear even when their order shifts.
grammarPoints.formation: [topic] は [time] [place] で [object] を [verb]. Keep the predicate at the end; phrase order before it can vary when the intended roles remain clear.
notes: Do not mechanically copy English subject–verb–object order.
Use particles to show each phrase’s role; the object marked を normally precedes its verb.
A sentence can omit an understood subject or topic.

examples.english: I read a book at home every day.
examples.japanese: 私は毎日家で本を読みます。
examples.kana: わたしはまいにちいえでほんをよみます。

schemas.instruction: Arrange the Japanese phrases and particles so the verb comes last.
schemas.context: Describe a routine at a particular place.
schemas.omission: Topic and time can be omitted if clear.
restrictions: Place the verb last.
Use a verb compatible with the selected object.

grammarPoints.title: Topic marker は
grammarPoints.meaning: は marks what a sentence is about. A topic need not be the grammatical subject, and は can contrast one topic with another.
grammarPoints.formation: Topic は comment. Besides a person, a time or an object can be the topic. For an object topic, は takes the place of を; a short “noun は？” invites the listener to comment.
notes: A topic is what the utterance is about; it need not be the actor.
は can introduce a topic for discussion or contrast it with another item.
Keep は on the phrase being contrasted, and do not stack をは in this beginner object-topic pattern.

examples.english: As for tomorrow, I will study.
examples.kana: あしたはべんきょうします。

examples.english: As for coffee, I do not drink it.
examples.japanese: コーヒーは飲みません。
examples.kana: コーヒーはのみません。

schemas.instruction: Set the stated person as the topic with は.
schemas.context: You are contrasting two people’s routines; the other person’s routine is already known.
schemas.english: Unlike the other person, {person} does not {activity}.
schemas.omission: Keep the contrasted topic explicit.
restrictions: Use は as the topic marker; it is pronounced wa.
The sentence illustrates a topic that is also the actor; the topic and grammatical subject do not always coincide.

schemas.context: The conversation has turned to what you will do at the stated time.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: The time is the topic; the understood actor is the speaker.

schemas.context: The listener asks about your habits concerning this drink.
schemas.english: As for {object}, I do not {verb} it.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: The drink is the topic, not the actor. Use は in place of を.
